# Draft:The Savage Hunt of King Stakh

The Savage Hunt for King Stakh is a 1979 Soviet Mystical-Horror film based on the story King Stakh's Wild Hunt by the Belarusian writer Vladimir Korotkevich .
The film is called the first Soviet mystical thriller and the first and only horror film made in Byelorussian SSR.
Filming of the ancient palace took place in Pidhirtsi Castle , which is located in the Lviv region ( Ukraine ).
The plot of the film differs significantly from the plot of the story on which it was based.
The film takes place in late 1900 in the Belarusian Polesie region , where a young ethnographer, Andrei Beloretsky, arrives to study local folklore . He settles on the Bolotnye Yalini estate, whose young owner, Nadezhda Yanovskaya, is the last representative of an ancient noble family and an orphan .
A ball is being held at the estate to celebrate the mistress's coming of age. Among the guests is Mr. Dubotovk, a local landowner, a joker, and Nadezhda Yanovskaya's guardian. He gives her a large painting of her ancestor, Roman Yanovsky, and a luxurious antique dress. At the ball, a conflict erupts between the young landowner Ales Vorona, who is courting Nadezhda, and Andrei Beloretsky, but it is quelled by Nadezhda and Dubotovk herself. The latter invites Andrei to stay at his estate.
The next day, Beloretsky learns the legend of the Little Man, the ghost of the Blue Woman who lives in the Marshy Yalins, and the Wild Hunt of King Stakh, a terrible hunt in which only people become game.
Legend tells of Stakh Gorski, a descendant of Grand Duke Alexander  —a young noble visionary. He desires to achieve independence for the Belarusian lands. He is loved and supported by peasants, the "forest brothers," and the best representatives of the national gentry. He possesses a talent for war, is courageous, decisive, and dreams of national happiness. He is trusting, generous, and noble: he readily forgives his enemy, the nobleman Roman Janowski, when the latter offers friendship, bestows gifts upon him, and, moreover, saves him from a swamp lynx during a hunt, risking his own life. But with a treacherous blow to the back of the head, Roman kills Stakh. Before his death, Stakh curses Janowski and his entire family down to the twentieth generation. The companions of the "peasant king" are also killed or seriously wounded. Tied to their horses, the dying freedom fighters are carried away into the night, changing their essence, calling upon the forces of darkness, and losing their original calling…
After this terrible incident, Roman Yanovsky perished in the Volotova Gap (according to legend, from King Stakh's Wild Hunt). Since then, many members of the Yanovsky family have perished for the same reason. They hear the hunting horn and are overtaken in the fields and swamps by Stakh's merciless, ghostly cavalry, from which there is no escape. Thus, Nadezhda Romanovna is the last representative of the Yanovsky line, and after her death, the palace and estate of Bolotnye Yaliny must be inherited by either her distant relative, Mrs. Kulsha, or her guardian, Ryhor Dubotovk.
Beloretsky doesn't believe everything he hears. However, he soon encounters some beggar children who tell him that one night, during King Stakh's Wild Hunt, hunters seized their parents, dragged them off to the swamp, and have not been seen since. This is also confirmed by Rygor, the serf of Mrs. Kulsha, who has gone mad with fear. However, Rygor points out that Stakh's cavalry is not phantom at all, but real, due to the manure left behind by the horses.
While Beloretsky was walking with a local acquaintance, Andrei Svetilovich, a former student at Kyiv University, someone shot at Beloretsky, wounding him in the arm. Soon after, Andrei Svetilovich died, before he could tell Beloretsky what he had learned, followed by Ignatiy Berman-Gatsevich, the manager of the Yanovsky estate. The police tried to hush up the matter as quickly as possible. After speaking with their representatives, Beloretsky realized they would be of no help. And his connection with Svetilovich, who sympathized with the revolutionaries, could have a negative impact on his life.
Andrei visits the Dubotovka estate, where he attends a batleika performance about King Stakh. There, he again clashes with Ales Vorona, escalating into a duel that ends with Ales being wounded.
Leaving the estate, near Marshy Yalin, Beloretsky stumbles upon King Stakh's Wild Hunt. The hunters pursue him, but he manages to evade them.
Little by little, Andrei uncovers the myth of the Little Man and the Blue Woman: the first was the dwarf Basil Gatcevich, the manager's brother, whom he was ashamed of and hid in the doll castle, and the second was Nadezhda Yanovskaya herself, who dressed in an old dress and wandered around the castle at night out of fear.
Then comes December. New Year's Eve is celebrated at the Bolotnye Yaliny estate .
But then the Wild Hunt begins again. The hunters catch and kill the actors of the traveling batleyka, as well as Mrs. Kulsha. The peasants, Beloretsky, and Ryhor encounter the hunters with stakes and scythes. During this hunt, it is revealed that most of the horsemen from Stakh's retinue are merely dummies in knightly attire, tethered to horses ridden by Ales Vorona. The cavalry is destroyed by the peasants, and Ales flees to the hunt's organizer, Dubotovk, to take refuge in his house. Dubotovk kills him, but soon dies himself when the peasants storm the estate and burn it down. It turns out that Dubotovk, using the legend of the Wild Hunt to remain above suspicion, has devised a plan to kill the last representatives of the Yanovsky family and seize all their property, as well as to keep the local superstitious people in fear.
It's January 1, 1901, the first day of the 20th century. On this day, Beloretsky is arrested for inciting rebellion and sent to St. Petersburg . Nadezhda Yanovskaya leaves with him.
A parable about man's victory over fear, told in the adventure genre, with unexpected, chilling events, exotic attributes of the setting and a romantic plot.
Korotkevich didn't come to the set and didn't interfere with the filming process. During the artistic council meeting, the writer noted that he wasn't entirely satisfied with the production, but he respected and accepted the director's right to his own interpretation of the work.
The film crew pondered for a long time how to convincingly show the "Wild Hunt" pursuit of the hero running through the swamp, until Rubinchik suggested filming the scene with a slow-motion camera to slow down the movements. A man had to be urgently sent to Minsk to get it . The red earth beneath the riders' feet was scorched with smoke bombs.
The film was shot in 1978–1979 in Belarus, Ukraine, and Russia. Pidhirtsi Castle in the Lviv region of the Ukrainian SSR was chosen as the castle for the Bolotnye Yalyny estate  . It is well known to moviegoers as the Royal Palace in the film " D'Artagnan and the Three Musketeers " by director Georgy Yungvald-Khilkevich.
Filming took place on location near Svirzh Castle in Lviv and in the Smolevichi District near Minsk, including at the Uruchye military training ground (sequences with fields  ), as well as in Alabino , near Moscow , where the equestrian scenes were performed by local cavalrymen. The interior of the castle and Mr. Dubotovka's house were partially filmed on the soundstages of the Belarusfilm studio.
The film also won several awards including:
* 1980, Italy — Grand Prix at the 1st International Film Festival of Detective and Mystery Films "Mistfest" in Cattolica
* 1980, France – Special Jury Prize for the film, Prize for Best Supporting Actress to V. Shendrikova at the 10th International Film Festival of Horror and Science Fiction Films in Paris
* 1980, Canada — Special Jury Prize at the IV Montreal International Film Festival
* 1981, Italy – Diploma for the film at the XIX International Science Fiction Film Festival in Trieste
* 1981, USA – Film diploma at the Filmex International Film Festival in Los Angeles
* 1983, Belgium – Grand Prix at the International Film Festival of Mysterious and Science Fiction Films “Passage 44” in Brussels  .
Cast and crew are:
* Boris Plotnikov  - Andrey Beloretsky, ethnographer
* Elena Dimitrova  as Nadezhda Romanovna Yanovskaya, owner of the Bolotnye Yaliny estate
* Albert Filozov  as Ignatius Berman-Gatsevich, manager of the Yanovsky estate
* Roman Filippov  as Mr. Ryhor Dubotovka
* Boris Khmelnitsky  - Ales Vorona
* Valentina Shendrikova  - widow of Mrs. Kulsha
* Alexander Kharitonov  as Andrey Svetilovich
* Igor Klass  - Rygor
* Vladimir Fedorov  as ''Basil Berman-Gatsevich, Ignatius's brother
* Maria Kapnist  - housekeeper
* Viktor Ilyichev  - bailiff
* Yuri Dubrovin  - forensic doctor
* Boris Romanov  - judicial investigator''
* Screenwriters and directors: Vladimir Korotkevich , Valery Rubinchik
* Operator: Tatyana Loginova
* Artist: Alexander Chertovich
* Costume designer: Eleonora Semenova
* Composer: Evgeny Glebov
* Sound engineer: Victor Morse
This film was released on DVD in 2006 by Ruscico and in 2025 Deaf Crocodile released the film on Blu-Ray which featured a brand-new restoration of the Director’s Cut of the film by Craig Rogers.
